name: Chloe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper pit, a 240-tonne Komatsu, and I'm lead operator on B crew, so eleven people answer to me on shift. Alarm goes at 4:10, bus leaves the square in Kellerton at 5, prestart checks by 6, then it's twelve hours of loading under the shovel, climbing the ramp and dumping at the crusher. I like it when the cycle runs smooth and the radio's quiet. What wears me out is nights, and the dust that gets in your teeth even with the cab sealed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You're lead operator at 27. How did that happen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just kept being the one who didn't put a truck in a ditch, honestly. Six years, no incidents, best load times on the crew, and I'm the union delegate for our pit as well. The pay doesn't match the title, though. Red Hill pays below the other mines because it's the only work for two hours in any direction, and they know it. Me and Marco rent above the bakery, I'm still paying off the car, and I send my mum a bit each month, so there's never more than a couple of weeks of money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing changes, which is fine by me. Red Hill already has enough computers telling us we're late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at tea break that I told you so. Every year some manager flies in with a new system that'll change everything, and every year we still need someone in the seat. I'd probably say it louder than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, because the driverless trucks are the thing that keeps me up, not chatbots. If AI stays a toy, my job is safe for as long as the copper lasts. But my pay still stays rubbish, so it's not like everything's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing, keep driving and keep the crew tight. Through the union I'd push the pay claim harder, because if the company saves time with these tools, some of that should land in our pockets. And I'd try to get the car paid off by next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit cheated that the boring version still means low pay, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the driverless trucks. Does this picture make them go away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the thing, they were here before anyone said AI. They've had them running at Copper Flats, the sister mine up north, for three years. In this picture they just stay a trial and don't creep across to us. That's what I'd be counting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pay claim actually ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four per cent and a proper night allowance. Right now night shift is two dollars more an hour, which doesn't even cover the coffee. If the company's saving minutes with their new scheduling software, I want those minutes paid back to the people driving.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew I said so: every year a manager flies in with a system that'll change everything, and every year someone still sits in the seat. I'd push the pay claim louder.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, because driverless trucks scare me more than chatbots. If AI stays a toy my job lasts as long as the copper, but my pay stays rubbish.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeping B crew tight, and uses her union role to push a four per cent claim and a better night allowance. Aims to pay off her car loan by next winter.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of resentment that the safe version still means low pay.
S0.quote: Right now night shift is two dollars more an hour, which doesn't even cover the coffee.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe separates AI from automation right away: the driverless haul trucks at the sister mine are her real fear, not software. Even in the calm picture she turns to pay, which shows how thin her margin is. The union role is central to how she sees herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's real, that's basically what's already starting. The question is whether it hits the trucks first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union meeting that any change has to be negotiated, not done to us. No driver loses their seat without a retraining place or a proper payout, full stop. I'd post the same thing on the union page, but politer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think haul trucks are the first thing to go, because a truck going up and down the same ramp is the easiest job in the pit for a robot. I'm the best driver on the crew and that won't matter at all. They don't need the best driver, they need no driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the regional organiser in the first month and ask for a written deal on automation, before the trucks arrive, not after. I'd stop the extras, no takeaway, no trip to the coast for Marco's birthday, and try to get one month of money in the bank. I won't go learning to babysit robots from a screen, though. That's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a knot in my stomach. I'm still in control in this one because there's time to fight, but I'd be thinking about it on every haul.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dale, he's 54, he's been driving since before I was born and he can't read a screen without his glasses on his forehead. If they offer the remote jobs, they'll go to young ones who play video games. Dale would just get the payout and sit in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn to run the robots. But if it's that or nothing, which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know how that sounds. If it's literally that or leaving Kellerton, I'd probably sit the course and hate every minute of it. But I'd make the union fight for the other option first, because a control room in the city isn't a job for anyone who lives here.

S1.say: Any change has to be negotiated, not done to us. No driver loses their seat without a retraining place or a proper payout, and I'd say that at the union meeting and online.
S1.think: Haul trucks will be the first to go because a ramp run is the easiest job in the pit for a robot. Being the best driver won't matter, because they don't need a driver at all.
S1.do: Goes to the regional union organiser in the first month to push for a written automation deal before trucks arrive. Cuts takeaways and a coast trip to build one month of savings, and only reluctantly considers remote-operation training if the alternative is leaving town.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach on every haul, though she still feels there's time to fight.
S1.quote: They don't need the best driver, they need no driver.
S1.fieldNote: Her skill gives her no comfort, which is striking for someone so proud of her record. She says she won't learn to run robots, then admits she would if the choice was leaving town. Her worry for older workers like Dale is genuine and shapes how she'd fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my car's even paid off. I don't know what you do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in and stop mines firing whole towns overnight. I'd be at every rally, I'd be on the phone to our member of parliament, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. Kellerton exists because of Red Hill, so if Red Hill doesn't need people, Kellerton is just houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in the mine and so is everyone I know. I don't have savings, there's nothing else in town, and I've never touched one of these AI things, so I'm starting from the bottom. That's the bit I'd not say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd get the union to demand redundancy pay at a proper rate, at least a year's wages, because that's the only lump of money I'd ever see. I'd tell Mum I can't send her anything for a while. Marco and I would look at moving to his brother's place in the city, but that only works if there's something for either of us there, and in this picture I don't know that there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums that don't add up. Two years isn't enough time to save, learn something, or even get angry properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years change compared with the slower pictures? What would you do in the time you've got?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no point retraining for anything, because whatever I learn the robot learns faster. So the only thing that matters is the payout and the politics. I'd spend every spare hour on the union, because that's the only thing I've got that a machine hasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you rang her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Mum, I can't do the hundred a month, I'm sorry. She'd say don't be silly, she'd manage. Then she'd skip her blood pressure tablets to make it work, and I'd know she was doing it.

S2.say: The government has to stop mines firing whole towns overnight. Kellerton exists because of Red Hill, so if Red Hill doesn't need people, Kellerton is just houses.
S2.think: I'm finished in the mine and so is everyone I know. No savings, nothing else in town, and I've never touched these AI tools, so I'd be starting from the bottom.
S2.do: Pushes the union in the first week to demand at least a year's wages in redundancy pay, stops sending money to her mum, and looks at moving to her partner's brother's place in the city. Spends her spare hours on union and political pressure rather than retraining.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep over money sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: Kellerton exists because of Red Hill, so if Red Hill doesn't need people, Kellerton is just houses.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning time removes retraining from her mind entirely; she sees the union and politics as the only levers left. The phone call with her mother brought out the most emotion. She blames the government for not protecting towns, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least I'd see the first truck drive itself before mine goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get the rules written, while there's still time. Every mine that automates should pay into a fund for the town, like a tax on each robot. I'd be pushing that at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm 32 when it lands. That's young enough to start again, but I'd have no money to start with. I'm scared I'd spend those five years fighting and then have nothing to show for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the car paid off and try to build up three months of savings, even if it means taking every overtime shift. I'd get my heavy rigid licence upgraded for the open road, because trucking on a highway might last a bit longer than trucking in a pit. And I'd keep the union busy on the robot tax idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but less frantic than the two-year one. It's like seeing a storm on the horizon instead of having the roof come off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the highway licence. Wouldn't the robots reach the highway too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, in five years. But it's a different company and maybe a different union, so at least I'd have a seat for a bit longer. I'm not pretending it's a real plan. It's more like buying time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years, compared with the two-year picture, actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get the car off my back and get a few thousand in the bank, that's it. And time for people to get organised, which matters more. With two years nobody has time to agree on anything, but with five you can get a law through.

S3.say: This is the moment to get rules written while there's still time. Every mine that automates should pay into a fund for the town, like a tax on each robot.
S3.think: I'd be 32 when it lands, young enough to restart but with no money to restart with. I'm scared of spending five years fighting and having nothing to show for it.
S3.do: Takes every overtime shift in the first year to pay off the car and save three months of expenses. Upgrades her licence to drive trucks on public roads to buy time, and keeps pushing a robot-tax fund through the union.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, but less frantic, like watching a storm on the horizon rather than losing the roof.
S3.quote: It's like seeing a storm on the horizon instead of having the roof come off.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years shift her from defence to a small plan: savings, a licence, and a policy idea. She openly calls the highway licence a way to buy time rather than a real plan. Her faith in collective action grows with the time available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole other life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly, so no excuses. The company, the government and the union should sit down now and plan who goes where. I'd say that in every meeting until they got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is the first one where I can picture myself coming out fine. I could train as a nurse or something like Marco's sister did. But I'd have to actually leave the pit, and I've never done anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for now, because the money is the money. I'd start a part-time course, maybe the community care certificate at the college annex in Kellerton, one night a week, so I've got something real in five years. And I'd keep the union pushing for a transition plan, because I won't be the only one who needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's still sad, but it's the kind of sad you can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually, the way my nan got a smartphone when the bank closed. I'd not go looking for it, but if the course needs it, I'd use it. I'm not proud of being slow, I just don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most, if you did leave the pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The radio, weirdly. Twelve hours of the crew teasing each other on channel four. You can't put that on a CV, but it's what keeps you awake at 3 in the morning.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to plan properly, so there are no excuses. The company, government and union should sit down now and decide who goes where.
S4.think: Ten years is the first picture where I can see myself coming out fine, maybe training in care work like Marco's sister. But I'd have to leave the pit, and I've never done anything else.
S4.do: Keeps driving for the income while starting a one-night-a-week community care certificate at the local college annex. Keeps the union pushing for a transition plan for the whole crew.
S4.feel: Uneasy: still sad, but a sadness she can live with.
S4.quote: You can't put that on a CV, but it's what keeps you awake at 3 in the morning.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Chloe moves from fighting to quietly planning an exit into care work. She admits her distrust of technology is not something she's proud of. The thing she'd miss is the crew's radio talk, not the machine or the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a proper payout, a year's wages at least, and some kind of fund that stays in Kellerton so the town doesn't just die. Money in my hand and somebody fighting for the town, that's it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Because if the people who live here owned even a bit of them, none of this would be so scary. It's not the machine I'm scared of, it's who it works for.

headlineQuote: It's not the machine I'm scared of, it's who it works for.
portrait: Chloe Dubois is a 27-year-old lead haul-truck driver at a copper pit, the union delegate for her crew, and someone with barely two weeks of money in the bank. She never uses AI tools and distrusts them, and her real fear is the driverless trucks already running at a sister mine. In the plateau picture she's calm but sore about pay; in the steady picture she's anxious and organising. Two-year AGI leaves her alarmed and focused only on payouts and politics, while five and ten years let her save, upgrade a licence and start a care course. Through it all she blames who owns the machines, not the machines themselves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to save or retrain and her town depends on the mine.
whatWouldHelp: A redundancy payout of at least a year's wages, and a fund that stays in the town so Kellerton doesn't die.
